paragraphs.title: Exile Is Not Divorce but the Result of Sin, and God’s Power Is Unlimited

answers: Because of their iniquities and transgressions
Because God was powerless
Because the people lacked water
easy.explanation: The KJV says, “for your iniquities have ye sold yourselves, and for your transgressions is your mother put away.”
easy.q: Why does the passage say that Israel was sold and put away?

answers: That the heavens can become dark
That He abandoned or sold Israel without cause
That the people needed water
easy.explanation: God asks whether He had sold or put away Israel as though He had abandoned them without a reason.
easy.q: What does God reject in His questions about the bill of divorcement and His creditors?

answers: Establish a king
Build cities
Dry up the sea and make the rivers a wilderness
easy.explanation: The KJV says, “at my rebuke I dry up the sea, I make the rivers a wilderness.”
easy.q: What can God do at His rebuke?

answers: The sins are presented as the cause of exile
The sins cancel God’s power
The sins only change the weather
medium.explanation: The passage directly connects Israel’s iniquities and transgressions with being sold and put away.
medium.q: What relationship does the passage establish between Israel’s sins and exile?

answers: Saving the people and then sending them into exile
Creating water and then drying it up
Drying up the sea, making rivers a wilderness, and causing fish to die of thirst
medium.explanation: Verse 2 describes the sea being dried up, rivers becoming a wilderness, and fish dying because there is no water.
medium.q: Which sequence describes God’s power in these verses?

answers: Bright light
Darkness and gloom
A strong wind
medium.explanation: “Blackness” refers to darkness and gloom covering the heavens.
medium.q: What does “blackness” mean in the phrase “I clothe the heavens with blackness”?

answers: They show that exile resulted from sin rather than arbitrary abandonment by God
They show that God needs someone else’s help
They describe a business agreement between two kings
challenge.explanation: God’s questions deny that He had rejected Israel without cause and point instead to their iniquities and transgressions.
challenge.q: Why are the questions about the bill of divorcement and creditors important to the message?

answers: God admits that He cannot act
The people do not need deliverance
The claim that God lacks power is immediately rejected
challenge.explanation: God asks whether His hand is shortened and then points to His power over the sea, rivers, and nature.
challenge.q: What does the contrast between “no power to deliver” and God’s drying up the sea teach?

answers: They all describe joy after exile
They emphasize judgment, mourning, and desolation
They describe the prophet’s commission
challenge.explanation: Dark heavens, sackcloth, drought, and dying fish create an image of mourning and destruction under God’s authority.
challenge.q: How do the blackness, sackcloth, and dryness support the main idea?

paragraphs.title: The Prophet’s Mission, Listening, and Suffering

answers: The tongue of the learned
A sword
Riches
easy.explanation: The speaker says, “The Lord God hath given me the tongue of the learned,” so he could speak a word in season to the weary.
easy.q: What did the Lord give the speaker so that he could speak to the weary?

answers: He rebelled against his mission
He was not rebellious and did not turn back
He hid his face
easy.explanation: He says, “I was not rebellious, neither turned away back.”
easy.q: What did the speaker do after the Lord opened his ear?

answers: Beatings, plucking of his cheeks, and spitting
Praise and gifts
Immediate rescue
easy.explanation: The passage says that he gave his back to the smiters and his cheeks to those who plucked off the hair, and that he was subjected to shame and spitting.
easy.q: What did the speaker suffer from his opponents?

answers: He learns to listen so that he can speak and encourage the weary
He prepares to run away
He listens only to his enemies
medium.explanation: The speaker is awakened morning by morning to hear as the learned, enabling him to speak a fitting word to the weary.
medium.q: How is the Lord awakening the speaker’s ear connected with his mission?

answers: Rebellion, flight, and finally listening
Receiving the mission, refusing to rebel, enduring suffering, and trusting God’s help
Hiding, remaining silent, and abandoning the mission
medium.explanation: The speaker receives a trained tongue and listening ear, remains obedient, suffers abuse, and trusts that the Lord will help him.
medium.q: Which sequence describes the speaker’s response to his mission and suffering?

answers: To punish the weary
To speak an appropriate and encouraging word to the weary
To hide the truth from the weary
medium.explanation: The phrase describes giving timely words of help and encouragement to someone who is weary.
medium.q: What does the phrase “speak a word in season to him that is weary” mean?

answers: Listening and learning are regular, continuing practices
The speaker acts only at night
The speaker does not need instruction
challenge.explanation: The repeated phrase emphasizes a continual pattern of awakening and listening to God’s instruction.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the repetition of “morning by morning”?

answers: Opposition makes the mission easy
The speaker abandoned his task
Faithfulness to a calling may involve suffering without canceling the calling
challenge.explanation: Although the speaker is mistreated, he remains obedient and does not turn back.
challenge.q: What does the contrast between the speaker’s encouraging mission and the blows he receives teach?

answers: It shows his willingness to face humiliation rather than flee
It shows that he could not hear God’s word
It shows that he concealed his mission
challenge.explanation: The speaker did not hide his face from shame and spitting, showing courageous endurance.
challenge.q: Why is “I hid not my face” significant in the description of the speaker’s suffering?

paragraphs.title: God Vindicates His Servant Against His Opponents

answers: His opponents
The Lord God
The people
easy.explanation: The speaker says, “He is near that justifieth me,” referring to the Lord God.
easy.q: Who is near the speaker and justifies him?

answers: His adversary
The fish
The heavens
easy.explanation: He asks, “who will contend with me?” and “who is mine adversary? let him come near to me.”
easy.q: Whom does the speaker invite to stand with him in judgment?

answers: They will grow strong forever
They will grow old and decay
They will rescue him
easy.explanation: They will “wax old as a garment,” and the moth will eat them up.
easy.q: What will happen to the speaker’s opponents?

answers: Because he has no opponents
Because he knows that the Lord is near and justifies him
Because he is physically stronger than they are
medium.explanation: His confidence rests on God’s nearness and His power to justify the speaker.
medium.q: Why is the speaker unafraid to face his opponents?

answers: God’s nearness, an invitation to judgment, confidence in help, and the opponents’ decay
Flight, hiding, sin, and exile
Drought, hunger, rain, and joy
medium.explanation: The passage moves from God’s justification to the speaker’s challenge and confidence, ending with the opponents’ destruction.
medium.q: Which sequence of ideas appears in these verses?

answers: The opponents will last forever
The opponents will wear out and disappear with time
The opponents will protect the speaker
medium.explanation: The worn garment and consuming moth symbolize the temporary and decaying nature of the opponents.
medium.q: What does the image of people growing old like a garment mean?

answers: To show that the speaker wants to escape judgment
To express confidence that opponents cannot prevail when God helps him
To show that the speaker does not know who opposes him
challenge.explanation: The questions challenge the opponents and express confidence in God’s vindication.
challenge.q: What is the purpose of the questions “Who will contend with me?” and “Who is mine adversary?”

answers: God’s help means the opponents cannot successfully condemn the speaker
God’s help causes the speaker to hide his face
The two ideas are unrelated
challenge.explanation: Because the Lord God helps the speaker, no opponent can finally condemn him.
challenge.q: What is the connection between “the Lord God will help me” and “who is he that shall condemn me?”

answers: The opponents are compared to a garment and a moth, both connected with wearing out or being consumed
The opponents are compared to the sea and rivers
The opponents are compared to light and morning
challenge.explanation: The garment grows old and the moth eats it, emphasizing the weakness and temporary nature of the opponents.
challenge.q: What easily overlooked detail appears in the final image?

paragraphs.title: Choosing Trust in God Over Self-Made Light

answers: Those who fear the Lord and obey the voice of His servant
Only those who never walk in darkness
Those who create their own fire
easy.explanation: The verse calls those who fear the Lord and obey His servant to trust in the Lord’s name.
easy.q: Who is called to trust in the name of the Lord?

answers: To walk in a condition without visible guidance or light
To celebrate in bright light
To travel across the sea
easy.explanation: The description refers to someone whose way is dark and who has no light.
easy.q: What does it mean to walk in darkness and have no light?

answers: They wait for the Lord’s light
They create their own fire and surround themselves with sparks
They put out every fire in the world
easy.explanation: The passage describes those who kindle a fire and compass themselves about with sparks they have kindled.
easy.q: What do the people who kindle a fire do?

answers: To trust in the Lord and stay upon his God
To create a larger fire
To stop obeying God’s servant
medium.explanation: Even without visible light, the person is told to trust in the Lord and rely upon God.
medium.q: What is required of someone who walks in darkness according to the passage?

answers: Those who trust in the Lord versus those who rely on their own self-made fire
Those who drink water versus those who eat bread
Prophets versus kings
medium.explanation: The verses contrast trusting God with depending on one’s own fire and sparks.
medium.q: What is the central contrast between the two groups in these verses?

answers: Small glowing pieces or flashes of fire
Garments
Rivers
medium.explanation: Sparks are small glowing pieces or flashes produced by fire.
medium.q: What does the word “sparks” mean in this context?

answers: Because a lack of visible light reveals whether a person relies on God or on personal strength
Because darkness eliminates the need for faith
Because darkness proves that the person has created fire
challenge.explanation: The command emphasizes trusting God even when no visible light or solution is present.
challenge.q: Why is the person walking in darkness told to trust in the Lord?

answers: Rest and security
Praise from the Lord
Lying down in sorrow
challenge.explanation: The warning concludes, “This shall ye have of mine hand; ye shall lie down in sorrow.”
challenge.q: What is the result of relying on one’s own fire?

answers: Self-made light may appear useful at first but does not provide true security
Self-made light always brings deliverance
Sorrow means great happiness
challenge.explanation: The passage warns that humanly created light cannot replace trust in God and ultimately leads to sorrow.
challenge.q: What does the movement from “light” to “sorrow” at the end of the passage suggest?
